title: Do Not Be Ashamed
sum: Paul writes from prison to Timothy, his "child". He thanks God for Timothy's sincere faith, which lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice, and urges him to stir up the gift he received through the laying on of Paul's hands. God's Spirit is not one of cowardice, so Timothy must not be ashamed of the message or of Paul in chains. The good news is about God's grace, given before time began and now brought into the open by Christ Jesus, who broke the power of death.

Paul is not ashamed either, because he trusts the one who will guard what has been entrusted until "that day". Timothy must hold to the sound words he heard and guard the good deposit with the Holy Spirit's help. The chapter ends with two pictures: all those in Asia have turned away from Paul, but Onesiphorus searched Rome until he found him and was not ashamed of his chain.
readings: Read as a personal letter, the chapter is full of feeling: tears, longing, memories of family, gratitude for a loyal friend and hurt at desertion. Paul writes as a father to a son he expects to leave behind, and the theme of shame runs through it: do not be ashamed (1:8), I am not ashamed (1:12), Onesiphorus was not ashamed (1:16).

Read as a testament, the chapter hands on a task. The deposit of teaching passes from the apostle to his successor (1:12-14), and the examples of the deserters and of Onesiphorus show what faithfulness and unfaithfulness look like. This reading is shared by those who hold that Paul wrote the letter and those who think a follower wrote it in his name.

views.H: The setting is a Roman prison (1:8, 16-17). Acts ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome (Acts 28:30-31); Eusebius (Church History 2.22) records what "is said": that Paul was released and later imprisoned again; he reads this letter as written then. Asia was the Roman province around Ephesus, where Paul had worked (Acts 19:10). Visiting a prisoner meant shame and risk, which is why Onesiphorus' visit is praised.
views.C: Critical scholars who think a follower wrote the Pastorals see in this chapter the main themes of the three letters: the "deposit" of teaching, "sound words", the "appearing" of Christ, and Paul as a model. They note that 2 Timothy is the most personal of the three, and some, such as P. N. Harrison in 1921, held that the personal passages (1:16-18 among them) preserve real notes from Paul. Those who hold Paul's authorship reply that the personal details are what one would expect in a real last letter.
views.L: The chapter follows the shape of Paul's letters: greeting (1:1-2), thanksgiving (1:3-5), and appeal (1:6-14), then personal news (1:15-18). The word "ashamed" ties the appeal together, and the pair of examples at the end (the deserters, Onesiphorus) closes it. 1:9-10 has the balanced style of an early confession.
views.J: Paul says he serves God "as my forebears did" (1:3), and the faith of two Jewish women, Lois and Eunice, comes first in Timothy's story (1:5; Acts 16:1). The wish for "mercy" and the hope for "that day" are drawn from the language of Israel's Scriptures.
views.T: 1:6 has been read in Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican teaching on ordination, and 1:16-18 in the debate over prayer for the dead. 1:9 is a favorite verse for the priority of grace.

deep.h: The deposit: what is guarded, and by whom
deep.b:
The word paratheke, "deposit", appears in 1:12 and 1:14 and in 1 Timothy 6:20. In the ancient world a deposit was property left in someone's keeping, to be returned whole; betraying a deposit was a serious crime. In 1:12 Paul is sure that God "has the power to guard my deposit until that day". In 1:14 Timothy must "keep the good deposit safe through the Holy Spirit".

Two readings of 1:12 have long been held. Many take "my deposit" as what Paul has entrusted to God: his life and his work, which God will keep through his death. Others, pointing to 1:14 and 1 Timothy 6:20, take it as what God has entrusted to Paul: the good news, which God will protect when Paul is gone. The letter as a whole joins both ideas: God keeps Paul, and God keeps the message through faithful people (2:2). The Plain English Translation keeps "my deposit" so that the reader can weigh the two.

The deposit language has played a part in the churches' debates about tradition. Catholic and Orthodox writers speak of the "deposit of faith" kept by the church; Protestant writers stress that the deposit is the apostolic teaching now found in Scripture. See the topic "Scripture, Tradition and Who Interprets".

echoes: Acts 16:1-3; Acts 19:10; Acts 20:37; Acts 24:14; Acts 28:16; Acts 28:20; Acts 28:30-31; 1 Corinthians 4:17; Romans 8:11; Romans 1:16; Ephesians 1:4; Ephesians 2:8-9; Titus 1:2; Titus 3:5; 1 Corinthians 15:53; 1 Timothy 4:14; 1 Timothy 6:20

settings.by: Paul, as the letter presents him: an apostle in prison in Rome
settings.to: Timothy, his coworker, probably at Ephesus (1:18; 4:12, 19), and through him the church there, since the letter's last words, "Grace be with you" (4:22), use the plural "you"
settings.when: if Paul wrote it, near the end of his life, in a Roman imprisonment, usually dated to the 60s; if a follower wrote it, some decades later
settings.why: To call Timothy to come quickly (4:9, 21), and above all to hand on to him the work and the teaching that Paul is about to leave: suffer for the good news, guard the deposit, entrust it to others, preach the word. The greeting's "promise of life" sets the tone for a letter written in the face of death.
settings.readers: Read in the church, the letter showed believers how Paul faced death and what he expected of those who came after him.
views: Paul wrote it in his last imprisonment in Rome, before his execution under Nero. Eusebius (Church History 2.22) already read it this way, passing on what "is said" of Paul's release and second imprisonment.
A follower wrote it after Paul's death, in the form of a farewell testament, to give Paul's authority to the teaching and the leaders of a later generation.
Paul's notes built into a later letter
The writer had real notes of Paul and added them to his letter, chiefly in the personal passages: the view of P. N. Harrison (1921).

settings.what: Thanksgiving and appeal: do not be ashamed
settings.when: while Paul is in chains (1:8, 16) and after many in Asia have turned away from him (1:15)
settings.why: To give Timothy courage. A young leader whose teacher is a prisoner might hide his connection with him, or shrink from suffering. Paul reminds him of his family's faith and of the gift he received, sets out the good news that is worth suffering for, and gives two examples: those in Asia who turned away and Onesiphorus who did not. Knowing that Timothy faced shame and danger by association makes "do not be ashamed" a concrete request, not a general virtue.

traditions.q: May Christians pray for the dead (1:16-18)?
views: Yes. The church has prayed for the dead from the beginning, above all by offering the Eucharistic sacrifice, so that the dead may be purified and reach the vision of God; the Catechism grounds this partly in the sacrifice Judas Maccabeus offered for the dead (2 Maccabees 12; Catechism 1030-1032).

Yes. The Confession of Dositheus (1672) teaches that the souls of the departed can be helped by the prayers of priests and by good works, "especially the unbloody Sacrifice" (Decree 18), without the Western doctrine of purgatory.

Lutherans do not forbid it. The Apology of the Augsburg Confession says that "the ancients speak of prayer for the dead, which we do not prohibit", but it rejects offering the Lord's Supper on behalf of the dead (Apology 24.94).
No. "Prayer is to be made for things lawful, and for all sorts of men living, or that shall live hereafter, but not for the dead" (Westminster Confession 21.4).

The burial rite of the Episcopal Church's Book of Common Prayer prays for the one who has died: "Rest eternal grant to him, O Lord", and "May his soul, and the souls of all the departed, through the mercy of God, rest in peace" (The Burial of the Dead, Rite One).

Yes. The United Methodist Church says its members commend the dead "to God's mercy at the resurrection", and its Book of Worship "includes some prayers for the dead", such as "We commend to your mercy all who have died, that your will for them may be fulfilled" (Ask The UMC, 2021).

title: A Good Soldier of Christ Jesus
sum: Paul tells Timothy to be strong in grace and to entrust what he heard to faithful people who can teach others. Three pictures follow: the soldier who serves the one who enlisted him, the athlete who keeps the rules, the farmer who works before he eats. Paul points to Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, and to his own chains: he is bound, but God's word is not. A short saying, perhaps a hymn, sums up the hope and the warning: if we died with him we will live with him; if we deny him he will deny us; if we are unfaithful, he stays faithful.

The second half turns to the false teachers. Timothy must not fight about words but teach the truth straight. Hymenaeus and Philetus say the resurrection has already happened, and their talk spreads like gangrene. Yet God's foundation stands, sealed with two sayings from Israel's Scriptures. Like a vessel kept clean for its owner, Timothy must flee youthful desires and pursue righteousness, and as the Lord's slave he must be gentle with his opponents, hoping God will give them repentance.
readings: A training manual for a leader
Read practically, the chapter tells a church leader how to work: hand on the teaching, endure, keep focused, study the word, avoid quarrels, correct gently.
A charge in a time of conflict

Read historically, the chapter answers a crisis: teachers in the church say the resurrection is past, and their teaching is spreading. Paul's answer is not a debate but a call to character and to the gospel of the risen Christ.

views.H: The three pictures come from daily life in the Roman world: soldiers enlisted for long service, the athletic games with their wreaths, farming. Paul's chains (2:9) and the word "criminal" recall how Christians were treated by Roman authorities. Hymenaeus is also named in 1 Timothy 1:20.
views.C: Critical scholars see in 2:2 a concern of the generation after the apostles: how to hand on teaching through trusted teachers. The saying in 2:11-13 is often taken as a quoted hymn. The claim that "the resurrection has already taken place" (2:18) has been compared with later teachers who held a spiritual resurrection.
views.L: The chapter moves in pairs: three images (2:3-6), the gospel of the risen Christ (2:8-13), the worker approved (2:14-19), the vessel (2:20-21), the gentle slave (2:22-26). The saying of 2:11-13 has four balanced lines, three that match and a fourth that breaks the pattern for effect.
views.J: The seal of 2:19 joins the Greek of Numbers 16:5, from the story of Korah's revolt, with phrases from Leviticus 24:16, Isaiah 26:13 and Sirach 17:26. 2:8 calls Jesus "from the offspring of David", the promised son of 2 Samuel 7. "The Lord's slave" (2:24) is the title of Moses and the prophets.
views.T: 2:2 is central in the churches' debates about apostolic succession. 2:11-13 is read in the debate about whether a believer can fall away. 2:15 in the KJV ("rightly dividing the word of truth") became a motto for Bible teachers.

deep.b:
"This saying is trustworthy" introduces four lines that many scholars take as a hymn or confession known in the churches:

If we died with him, we will live with him too;
if we hold out, we will also reign with him;
if we deny him, he will deny us as well;
if we are unfaithful, he stays faithful.

The first two lines are promises and the third a warning, each matching what we do with what Christ will do. The fourth breaks the pattern: our unfaithfulness is not answered with his. The added words "for he cannot deny himself" may be the writer's comment on the hymn. The lines echo Romans 6:8 (dying and living with Christ) and Jesus' saying about denial (Matthew 10:33; Luke 12:9).

Readers have heard the hymn at baptism (dying with Christ in the water) and at martyrdom (dying for Christ), and both settings fit a letter written from prison. The tension between the third and fourth lines is at the heart of the churches' debate on perseverance; the card on this page sets out the answers.

echoes: Numbers 16:5; Numbers 16:26; Leviticus 24:16; Isaiah 26:13; Sirach 17:26; 2 Samuel 7:12-16; Romans 1:3-4; Romans 6:8; Romans 9:21; Matthew 10:33; Luke 12:9; 1 Corinthians 9:7; 1 Corinthians 9:24-25; 1 Corinthians 15:12; Acts 11:18; Acts 28:31; 1 Timothy 1:20; Proverbs 3:6

settings.what: Hand it on, and suffer with me
settings.when: the same letter, while Paul is in chains (2:9)
settings.why: To prepare Timothy for leadership after Paul: to train trustworthy teachers who can train others (2:2), and to accept hardship as a soldier, athlete and farmer do. The appeal to "remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead" gives the reason to endure: the gospel of a risen Lord who was descended from David.
views: The instructions are personal, for Timothy in his situation.
A rule for every church leader
The letter shapes a pattern for leaders in every generation.

settings.by: Quoted by Paul; probably a hymn or confession already used in the churches
settings.to: Timothy, and every believer who sang or said it
settings.when: perhaps used at baptism or in worship
settings.why: To remind believers under pressure that dying with Christ leads to life with him, that endurance leads to reigning, that denial is serious, and that Christ's faithfulness does not depend on ours.

settings.to: Timothy, as the church's teacher, with Hymenaeus and Philetus in view (2:17)
settings.when: while a teaching that the resurrection was past was spreading
settings.why: To show Timothy how to deal with error: by teaching the true word accurately, avoiding pointless quarrels, keeping himself clean, and correcting opponents gently in the hope that God will change them. The local crisis explains the tone: the danger is not argument as such but a teaching that eats away at faith.

traditions.q: Does 2:2 (with 1:6) describe a succession of ordained ministers from the apostles?
views: Yes. Bishops are "transmitters of the apostolic line", and the apostles "by the imposition of hands ... passed on to their auxiliaries the gift of the Spirit"; the Catechism gives 2 Timothy 1:6-7 as one of its texts for this (Catechism 1555-1556).
Yes. The bishop stands as a successor of the apostles, and the episcopate has come down "by a continued succession"; only a bishop ordains priests (Confession of Dositheus, Decree 10).

The Episcopal Church's Book of Common Prayer says that "from the apostles' time, there have been different ministries within the Church", that bishops "carry on the apostolic work of leading, supervising, and uniting the Church", and that "It has been, and is, the intention and purpose of this Church to maintain and continue these three orders" (Preface to the Ordination Rites).

Lutherans keep church order and its ranks as an arrangement made by human authority. No one should publicly teach or give the sacraments "unless he be regularly called" (Augsburg Confession 14); the Apology says "it is our greatest wish to maintain church-polity and the grades in the Church", "even though they have been made by human authority", and blames the bishops for its breakdown (Apology 14.24-25).

God taught and governed the church through the apostles, and "through their successors he has taught and governed the Church unto this day", but "the one and an equal power or function is given to all ministers"; those elected "are to be ordained by the elders with public prayer and laying on of hands" (Second Helvetic Confession 18).

traditions.q: Can a true believer finally fall away (2:12-13)?
views: No one may promise himself perseverance with absolute certainty, unless by special revelation; God will finish the good work unless people fail his grace (Council of Trent, session 6, chapter 13 and canon 16).

A baptized believer can fall into many sins and is restored through repentance and the mystery of penance (Confession of Dositheus, Decree 16); the Confession does not teach a doctrine of eternal security.
Yes. The Augsburg Confession condemns those "who deny that those once justified can lose the Holy Ghost" (Article 12).
No. Those whom God has effectually called and sanctified "can neither totally nor finally fall away from the state of grace" (Westminster Confession 17.1).
Yes. "After we have received the Holy Ghost, we may depart from grace given, and fall into sin, and, by the grace of God, rise again" (Articles of Religion 12).
No. "All true believers endure to the end" and will never fall away from the state of grace (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 5).

title: All Scripture Is God-Breathed
sum: "In the last days hard times will set in." Paul lists the vices of people who love themselves, money and pleasure rather than God, who keep the outward form of godliness but deny its power. Some of them slip into households and capture women burdened by sins, always learning but never coming to the truth. Like Jannes and Jambres, the magicians who opposed Moses, they stand against the truth, but their folly will be exposed.

Timothy is different. He has followed Paul's teaching and way of life, and seen his sufferings at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra, from which the Lord rescued him. Everyone who wants to live a godly life in Christ will be persecuted. So Timothy must remain in what he learned from those he trusts, and in the holy writings he has known since childhood, which can make him wise for salvation through faith in Christ. Every Scripture is God-breathed and useful, so that God's servant is equipped for every good work.
readings: Some read 3:1-9 as a prophecy of the time just before Christ's return, and look for its signs in their own society.
Most read the "last days" as the time the church already lives in. The people described are already at work (3:5-9), and Timothy is told to turn away from them now.
3:14-17 is read on its own as the Bible's key text on Scripture: its origin in God (God-breathed) and its purpose (teaching, correction, training, equipping).

views.H: The house churches met in homes, so traveling teachers moved from household to household (3:6). The persecutions at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra (3:11) are told in Acts 13-14, in the region of Timothy's home (Acts 16:1-2). Timothy's Jewish upbringing explains his knowledge of the Scriptures from childhood (3:15).
views.C: The vice list (3:2-5) is a standard form in Greek and Jewish moral writing. Critical scholars see the "weak women" of 3:6-7 as reflecting the writer's concern for household order and his scorn for women attracted to rival teachers. On 3:16 scholars discuss whether the Greek means "every Scripture is God-breathed" or "every God-breathed Scripture is useful". The manuscripts do not differ in that clause.
views.L: The list of vices is framed by "lovers" words: lovers of self and of money at the start, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God at the end. 3:10-11 lists Paul's teaching and life in nine nouns. The chapter sets the false teachers (3:1-9) against Timothy (3:10-17): "But you" (3:10, 14).
views.J: Jannes and Jambres are named in Jewish tradition, not in Exodus: in the Damascus Document, the Targum, and the Talmud. "The holy writings" (3:15) are the Jewish Scriptures, probably in Greek. "The man of God" (3:17) is the title of Moses and the prophets.
views.T: 3:16-17 is the most cited text in the churches' teaching on Scripture: its inspiration, its authority, and for some its freedom from error. Churches agree that Scripture is God-breathed; they differ on its relation to tradition, on which books it includes, and on what inspiration implies. See the card.

deep.b:
The sentence in 3:16 is short and has no verb in the Greek: pasa graphe theopneustos kai ophelimos, "every Scripture God-breathed and useful". The Plain English Translation supplies "is" and reads "Every Scripture is God-breathed and useful", as most translations do. The American Standard Version (1901) reads "Every scripture inspired of God is also profitable". In both readings the Scriptures in view are God-breathed. The manuscripts do not differ in this clause: Codex Sinaiticus and all the printed editions read the same words. (Later in the verse the Byzantine text has another form of the word for "exposing"; see the variant.)

What "God-breathed" says. The word theopneustos is found only here in the Bible. It says that Scripture comes from God, as breath comes from a mouth. It does not describe how the human writers worked. 2 Peter 1:21 adds that "people borne along by the Holy Spirit spoke from God".

What "Scripture" meant. For Timothy, "Scripture" was what he had known since childhood, "the holy writings" of Israel (3:15), read probably in Greek. The churches apply the verse to the New Testament as well; 1 Timothy 5:18 and 2 Peter 3:16 already show Christian sayings and Paul's letters being placed beside the older Scriptures.

What Scripture is for. The verse stresses usefulness: teaching, exposing wrong, putting things right, training in righteousness, so that "the man of God" is "equipped for any good work". The aim is a life, not only a doctrine.

What the churches built on it. Catholic teaching holds that the books of Scripture, written under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit by human authors who are "true authors", teach "solidly, faithfully and without error" the truth God wanted put into the sacred writings "for the sake of salvation" (Dei Verbum 11). The Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978), an evangelical statement, affirms that "Scripture in its entirety is inerrant" and that inspiration "strictly speaking, applies only to the autographic text" (Articles 10, 12). The card on this page sets the churches side by side.

echoes: Exodus 7:11-12; Exodus 7:22; Exodus 8:18-19; Exodus 9:11; Numbers 22:22; Acts 13:50; Acts 14:5; Acts 14:19-22; Acts 16:1-2; Romans 1:29-31; Romans 2:20; Romans 15:4; 2 Peter 1:20-21; 2 Peter 3:3; Jude 1:18; Deuteronomy 33:1; 1 Kings 17:18

settings.what: The last days and the false teachers
settings.to: Timothy, with the false teachers in the house churches in view
settings.when: while teachers were moving through the households of the church (3:6)
settings.why: To show Timothy that the troubles he faced were not a surprise but the expected mark of "the last days", and to tell him to turn away from such people (3:5). The comparison with Pharaoh's magicians reassures him: imitation of the truth will be exposed. Knowing that the warning was about people already present keeps the passage from being read only as a forecast of a distant future.
views: The "last days" are the church's present, and the people described are Timothy's opponents.
The passage describes the time just before Christ's return, with Timothy's opponents as an early sign.

settings.why: To anchor Timothy in two things the false teachers lacked: a life he had seen (Paul's teaching, conduct and sufferings) and the Scriptures he had known since childhood. The famous statement about Scripture (3:16-17) is given to a young leader as a tool for his work: Scripture equips him for every good work. Knowing this setting shows that the passage was first meant to strengthen a teacher, not to settle later debates, though the churches have rightly drawn on it.

traditions.q: What does it mean that Scripture is God-breathed (3:16), and how far does its authority reach?
views: Scripture is written under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit by human authors who are true authors, and teaches "solidly, faithfully and without error" the truth God wanted put down "for the sake of salvation"; it is read with Tradition and the church's teaching office (Dei Verbum 11).

Scripture is "God-taught" and is to be believed as the Catholic Church (by which the Confession means the Orthodox Church) has interpreted and handed it on; the church's witness is "not of inferior authority" to Scripture's. The canon includes books such as Sirach and the Maccabees (Confession of Dositheus, Decree 2 and Question 3).

The prophetic and apostolic Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments are "the sole rule and standard according to which all dogmas together with [all] teachers should be estimated and judged"; the creeds and confessions are witnesses, "not judges, as are the Holy Scriptures" (Formula of Concord, Epitome, Rule and Norm 1, 8).

The books of the Old and New Testaments are "given by inspiration of God, to be the rule of faith and life", and their authority depends "wholly upon God ... the author thereof", not on any church (Westminster Confession 1.2, 1.4).
"Holy Scripture containeth all things necessary to salvation", so nothing that cannot be read in it or proved by it may be required as an article of faith (Article 6).
Wesley's Articles of Religion repeat the Anglican article: Scripture contains all things necessary to salvation (Article 5).
The Bible "was written by men divinely inspired" and has "truth, without any mixture of error" for its matter (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 1).

"The Scriptures, both the Old and New Testaments, are verbally inspired of God and are the revelation of God to man, the infallible, authoritative rule of faith and conduct" (Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths 1, which cites 2 Timothy 3:15-17). Its 2015 position paper adds that "Strict inerrancy is claimed only for the original writings".

The Chicago Statement (1978), drawn up by more than 200 evangelical leaders from a variety of denominations, is not a church's confession but a statement many evangelicals accept. It affirms that the whole of Scripture and all its parts were given by divine inspiration, that God used the writers' personalities and styles, that inspiration applies strictly to the original texts, and that "Scripture in its entirety is inerrant" (Articles 6, 8, 10, 12).

title: I Have Kept the Faith
sum: Before God and Christ Jesus, the coming Judge, Paul gives Timothy his last charge: proclaim the word at every time, with patience, because people will turn from sound teaching to teachers who say what they want to hear. Timothy must keep a clear head, endure, and finish his ministry. Paul's own end is near: he is being poured out like a drink offering, he has competed in the good contest, finished the race and kept the faith, and the crown of righteousness waits for him and for all who love Christ's appearing.

The letter closes with news and requests. Demas has deserted, others are away, only Luke is with Paul. Timothy must bring Mark, the cloak left at Troas, and the scrolls and parchments. At Paul's first defense no one stood by him, but the Lord did, and he was rescued from the lion's mouth; the Lord will bring him safely into his heavenly kingdom. Greetings follow, and a last plea: come before winter.
readings: Read as a farewell, 4:6-8 is the climax of the letter and of Paul's life, like the last words of Moses, Joshua and David to their successors (Deuteronomy 31; 1 Kings 2:1-9) and Paul's own farewell to the Ephesian elders (Acts 20:17-38).
A real letter with real errands
Read as a working letter, the chapter's lists of names, places and requests (a cloak, books, Mark) show a prisoner arranging his affairs and asking for help before winter.

views.H: Paul has had a "first defense" in a Roman court (4:16) and expects death (4:6). Tradition, recorded by Eusebius (Church History 2.22 and 2.25), says he was beheaded in Rome under Nero. Sea travel stopped in winter (4:21; Acts 27:9). Troas, Miletus, Corinth, Thessalonica, Galatia and Dalmatia map the network of Paul's coworkers.
views.C: The personal details of 4:9-21 are the strongest argument for Paul's authorship, or at least for genuine Pauline notes in the letter, as P. N. Harrison argued. Critics reply that such details were part of letters written in an author's name. The travels implied (Trophimus at Miletus, the cloak at Troas) do not fit Acts, so they point either to a journey after Acts 28 or to a later writer.
views.L: 4:6-8 is built from images: the drink offering, the departure, the contest, the race, the crown. The verb "love" ties 4:8 ("all who have set their love on his appearing") to 4:10 (Demas "loved the present age"). The letter ends, as Paul's letters do, with greetings and grace.
views.J: The drink offering (4:6) is the wine poured out with Israel's sacrifices (Numbers 28:7). "The lion's mouth" (4:17) echoes Psalm 22:21, and "the Lord will pay him back" (4:14) echoes Psalm 62:12 and Proverbs 24:12 in the Greek. The farewell recalls the testaments of Moses and David.
views.T: 4:7-8 is cited in the debates about merit and reward. 4:21 (Linus) was cited by Irenaeus in the list of bishops of Rome. 4:16 ("may it not be held against them") is a pattern of forgiveness.

deep.h: Paul's last words and the farewell testament
deep.b:
Many scholars, both those who hold that Paul wrote the letter and those who do not, read 2 Timothy as a testament or farewell speech: a dying leader hands on his task. The Bible has many such scenes. Moses charges Joshua ("Be strong and bold", Deuteronomy 31:7); David tells Solomon, "I am going the way of all the earth. So be strong. Be a man" (1 Kings 2:2); Paul tells the Ephesian elders that "vicious wolves will get in among you" after he is gone (Acts 20:29). Jewish writings outside the Bible, such as the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, are built on the same pattern.

The features of the form are all here: the leader's coming death (4:6), a look back over his life (4:7; 3:10-11), warnings about the future (3:1-5; 4:3-4), the charge to a successor (4:1-5), and the handing on of teaching (1:13-14; 2:2). Readers who hold that a follower wrote the letter take the form as a clue: the writer chose the testament to give Paul's last word to a later generation. Readers who hold that Paul wrote it say that a man about to die would naturally write in this way.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the two loves of chapter 4
deep.b: The verb "love" appears twice in this chapter, and the letter seems to set the two uses against each other on purpose. The crown goes to "all who have set their love on his appearing" (4:8); two verses later Demas has left: "He loved the present age" (4:10). Both are perfect or aorist forms of the same verb, agapao. The contrast may be the letter's own diagnosis of desertion: Demas did not stop loving, he loved the wrong age. Read this way, 4:8-10 restates the theme of 3:2-4, where people love themselves, money and pleasure rather than God, in two people's lives. The suggestion that this contrast is the key to the chapter is mine, and it rests only on the repeated verb.

settings.what: The last charge and the farewell
settings.when: after Paul's first defense (4:16), with death near (4:6)
settings.why: To pass the work to Timothy under oath before God and the coming Judge, and to show him how to finish: Paul's own life is the model, a contest finished and a faith kept. The crown promised to "all who have set their love on his appearing" includes Timothy and every reader. Knowing that these were written as the words of a condemned man gives them their weight.
views: Paul wrote them shortly before his execution.
A follower shaped Paul's farewell for a later generation, as Jewish and Greek writers composed testaments of great figures.

settings.to: Timothy, and the church with him (the plural "you" of "Grace be with you", 4:22)
settings.why: To bring Timothy (and Mark) to Rome quickly, to warn him about Alexander, to tell him who has left and who remains, and to pass on greetings. These lines show a network of coworkers spread from Galatia to Dalmatia and a prisoner in need of practical help: a cloak, books, friends.
